screened.title: To RAG, or Not to RAG? A Comparative Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for ICD Coding of German Tumor Diagnoses
screened.criterion: All four hold; criterion 2 is the pivotal one (an LLM/RAG arm, not solely a supervised encoder, performs the coding). Criterion 1 satisfied by free-text clinical tumor diagnosis descriptions, criterion 3 by its own exact/partial-match accuracy figures, criterion 4 by it being a full IMRaD preprint.
screened.evidence_quote: We evaluated nine different embedding models using similarity search and embedding-based classification, as well as LLM-based coding, with and without RAG, on a real-world dataset of 2,024 unique German tumor diagnosis descriptions labeled with ICD-10 and ICD-O topography codes.
screened.coder_mechanism: Hybrid comparison: embedding-based similarity search / embedding classification (nine embedding models, best = Qwen3-Embedding-8B) versus generative LLM coding with and without retrieval augmentation (Llama 3.1 8B and Llama 3.3 70B, base and fine-tuned), with a retrieval knowledge base built from Alpha-ID, ICD-10-GM and ICD-O-3 classifications. The LLM/RAG arm is a genuine coder built and evaluated by the authors, so the eligible mechanism is present.
screened.text_type: German-language free-text tumor diagnosis descriptions drawn from real-world clinical documentation (2,024 unique descriptions), labelled with ICD-10(-GM) and ICD-O-3 topography codes.
screened.note: Abstract obtained from the Crossref work record (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.64898/2026.05.27.26353695); the doi.org and medRxiv HTML landing pages were unreachable during this session due to a transient tool outage, but Crossref returned the full structured Introduction/Methods/Results/Conclusion abstract and confirms type = posted content (preprint), institution medRxiv/openRxiv. Two borderline points, neither disqualifying under the pre-registered rule: (a) the coded units are short diagnosis descriptions rather than full discharge summaries, but the abstract explicitly frames them as "free-text clinical documentation" about tumor diagnoses, which is clinical free text about a patient; (b) the paper is comparative in framing, but it is not an excluded benchmark/dataset paper — the authors construct their own retrieval knowledge base and fine-tune their own RAG models, and make accuracy claims about those systems (47.8% exact / 72.1% partial for ICD-10 with embedding classification; 80.6% partial for ICD-10 with RAG on Llama 3.3 70B). Note for extraction: the best exact-match result comes from the non-eligible embedding arm, so if the audit records "best system" characteristics, flag that this study's headline exact-match number is not from the LLM/RAG coder.
screened.adjudicator_reason: Refutation attempted on all four criteria and failed. (2) The pivotal mechanism criterion holds: this is not solely a supervised encoder. The authors build and evaluate a generative arm — "LLM-based coding, with and without RAG" using base and fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B and Llama 3.3 70B over a retrieval knowledge base they constructed from Alpha-ID/ICD-10-GM/ICD-O-3 — and report its own accuracy (80.6% partial-match ICD-10, 75.0% ICD-O with Llama 3.3 70B). The embedding similarity-search/classification arm is a comparator, not the only coder. (1) Inputs are clinical free text about patients: "Coding tumor diagnoses from free-text clinical documentation currently requires substantial manual effort"; 2,024 unique German free-text tumor diagnosis descriptions from real-world clinical documentation, with ICD-10/ICD-O topography codes assigned to them — not drug labels, death registers, trial descriptions, or code-to-name interpretation, and not phenotyping (output is an assigned code, not a patient label). (3) Explicit exact- and partial-match accuracy claims about its own systems. (4) Full structured IMRaD medRxiv preprint, not an abstract, poster, editorial, or protocol; preprints are not on the exclusion list. The "benchmark/dataset that does not itself build a coder" exclusion does not apply because the authors fine-tuned models and built the RAG pipeline themselves. Caveat for the pool: the same group has arXiv 2510.13624 (instruction-tuning on public catalogues) apparently on the same dataset — check the duplicate rule if both are present, though they report different systems.

screened.title: Fine-tuning for accuracy: evaluation of Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) for automatic assignment of International Classification of Disease (ICD) codes to clinical documentation
screened.criterion: All four hold; criterion 2 is the pivotal one (the coder is a generative LLM, GPT-3.5 Turbo, not a supervised encoder), with criteria 1, 3 and 4 also satisfied and no named exclusion triggered.
screened.evidence_quote: Initially the target ICD-10 code was present in the assigned codes by the default GPT-3.5 Turbo model in 29.7% of the cases. After fine-tuning with 100 notes for each top code, the accuracy improved to 62.6%.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM — GPT-3.5 Turbo called through the OpenAI API, evaluated both zero-shot (default model) and after supervised fine-tuning of the same generative model. No retrieval component and no BERT-family encoder classifier is described.
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about patients: 2,000 clinical notes (discharge summaries) drawn from MIMIC-IV, 200 per each of the ten most prevalent ICD-10 codes, split 100 train / 100 test per code.
screened.note: Criterion 1: ICD-10 codes assigned to MIMIC-IV clinical notes — "Assignment of International Classification of Disease (ICD) codes to clinical documentation is a tedious but important task that is mostly done manually." Criterion 2: the assigning mechanism is GPT-3.5 Turbo itself; fine-tuning a generative LLM does not convert it into the excluded "supervised encoder/classifier" category (which targets BERT/RoBERTa/BioClinicalBERT classifiers). Criterion 3: explicit accuracy claim about its own system (29.7% zero-shot to 62.6% fine-tuned). Criterion 4: full research article in Journal of Medical Artificial Intelligence, 2024, with structured Background/Methods/Results/Conclusions — not an abstract, poster or editorial. It builds and evaluates a coder rather than merely releasing a benchmark, and the LLM assigns codes to notes rather than interpreting existing codes, so no exclusion applies. Caveat for the audit record: evaluation is a restricted top-10-code setup scored by whether the single target code appears among the assigned codes, not full multi-label MIMIC coding — relevant to comparability, not to eligibility. Retrieval note: doi.org redirected via jmai.amegroups.com to https://jmai.amegroups.org/article/view/9040/html (article view 9040, not 9636).
screened.adjudicator_reason: Verified against the publisher version of record (JMAI Vol 7, 30 Jun 2024, Original Article). All four criteria hold and no refutation succeeded. (1) Clinical free text about patients: MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries, 200 notes for each of the ten most prevalent ICD-10 codes, split 100 train / 100 test. (2) Coder mechanism is a generative LLM: GPT-3.5 Turbo prompted via the OpenAI API to assign ICD-10 codes, then the same generative model after supervised fine-tuning; no BERT-family encoder classifier and no retrieval component appears anywhere, so the "supervised encoder mislabeled as LLM" failure mode does not apply, and fine-tuning a generative LLM does not make it "solely a supervised encoder/classifier". (3) Explicit accuracy claim about its own system: 29.7% default rising to 62.6% fine-tuned. (4) Full Original Article with Background/Methods/Results/Conclusions, not an abstract, editorial, or protocol. Checked exclusions: it is not a review/survey/benchmark (it builds its own coder), the LLM assigns codes to notes rather than interpreting or querying existing codes, the text is clinical rather than regulatory/label/registry, the target terminology is ICD-10, and the output is a code set rather than a phenotype label. An earlier Research Square preprint (rs-4392229/v1) reports the same system by the same group; under the duplicate rule the fullest version is this peer-reviewed article, so this record is the one to keep.

screened.title: Developing an ICD-10 Coding Assistant: Pilot Study Using RoBERTa and GPT-4 for Term Extraction and Description-Based Code Selection
screened.criterion: Criterion 2 (coding mechanism) is the decisive one; criteria 1, 3, 4 also satisfied
screened.evidence_quote: Using a RAG approach, ICD codes were assigned to the lead terms by querying a vector database of ICD code descriptions with OpenAI's text-embedding-ada-002 model.
screened.coder_mechanism: hybrid — RoBERTa NER extracts lead terms only; the codes themselves are ASSIGNED by a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline (GPT-4 generates code descriptions from the extracted textual evidence; text-embedding-ada-002 vector search over an ICD code-description database performs the assignment). The supervised encoder is a pre-step, not the coder, so the "solely a supervised encoder" exclusion does not bite.
screened.text_type: clinical free text about patients — 1000 Spanish clinical case reports from the CodiEsp-X (CodiEsp challenge explainability) dataset, annotated with ICD-10 diagnosis and procedure codes
screened.note: Full paper, JMIR Formative Research 2025;9:e60095 (11 Feb 2025), Puts, Zegers, Dekker, Bermejo; PMC11835781. Abstract read verbatim from PubMed Central after the publisher DOI landing page was unavailable. Criterion 1 met: "The explainability dataset from the CodiEsp challenge (CodiEsp-X) was used, featuring 1000 Spanish clinical cases annotated with ICD-10 codes." Criterion 3 met on both counts — accuracy AND explainability claims about its own system: "The fine-tuned Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach achieved an overall F1-score of 0.80 for ICD lead term extraction on the new CodiEsp-X-lead dataset... the overall explainability F1-score for the CodiEsp-X task was limited to 0.305, significantly lower than the state-of-the-art F1-score of 0.633." Criterion 4 met: full JMIR original-paper article, not an abstract/poster. Two near-miss exclusions checked and rejected: (a) the paper releases a derived dataset (CodiEsp-X-lead) but is not a benchmark-only record — it builds and evaluates its own coding assistant; (b) code descriptions are used as the RAG corpus, but the system assigns codes TO a note rather than merely interpreting or querying existing codes, so the "LLM interprets existing codes" exclusion does not apply. Note the result is a negative one (RAG code assignment underperformed), which is irrelevant to eligibility — the rule requires an accuracy/explainability claim, not a favourable one. Same group as other Puts/Dekker/Bermejo ICD work; if another record in the set reports this same RoBERTa+GPT-4 CodiEsp-X system, apply the duplicate rule and keep this full JMIR version over any preprint (a ResearchGate preprint of the same title exists and should be dropped if separately captured).
screened.adjudicator_reason: Refutation attempt failed; all four criteria hold. (1) Clinical free text: 1000 Spanish clinical case reports about patients from CodiEsp-X, annotated with ICD-10 diagnosis and procedure codes — not drug labels, registers, or trial text. (2) Mechanism: the supervised RoBERTa is confined to NER of lead terms and never emits a code; assignment is performed by an explicit RAG pipeline — GPT-4 generates code descriptions from the textual evidence, text-embedding-ada-002 retrieves candidates from a vector database of ICD code descriptions, and GPT-4 then selects the best-matching ICD code from the 50 retrieved candidates. This is an LLM/RAG coder, so the "solely a supervised encoder/classifier" exclusion does not bite; nor is it phenotyping or code-interpretation, since the output is an assigned ICD code set for a note. (3) Accuracy/explainability claims about its own system: F1 0.80 for lead-term extraction, overall explainability F1 0.305 vs 0.633 state of the art, ~5% reduction in retrieval failures from GPT-4-generated descriptions. (4) Full original paper in JMIR Formative Research 2025;9:e60095, not an abstract or poster; an earlier JMIR preprint under a different title is the same system by the same group, and this published version is the fullest and should be the retained record.

screened.title: Challenges and Solutions in Applying Large Language Models to Guideline-Based Management Planning and Automated Medical Coding in Health Care: Algorithm Development and Validation
screened.criterion: 2 (decisive); all four criteria hold — 1 (ICD-10 assigned to MIMIC-IV admission documentation), 2 (LLM + vector-retrieval pipeline, not a supervised encoder), 3 (own-system recall claim with significance test), 4 (full peer-reviewed "Algorithm Development and Validation" paper)
screened.evidence_quote: GAVS was evaluated on 958 randomly selected admissions from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)–IV database, in which billed International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes served as the ground truth.
screened.coder_mechanism: Hybrid LLM + retrieval (RAG-style): "generation-assisted vector search" (GAVS) — GPT-4.1 is prompted to generate granular diagnostic entities, each of which is embedded on the fly and matched to the official ICD-10 ontology by cosine-similarity semantic search. Explicitly not a trained/supervised classifier. (A second framework in the same paper, GARAG, is a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline for guideline-based management planning — not a coder.)
screened.text_type: Clinical documentation for MIMIC-IV inpatient admissions (patient-level clinical text), coded to ICD-10 against billed codes as ground truth. The abstract does not name the specific note type (e.g. discharge summary); the full text likewise does not state it explicitly in the section retrieved.
screened.note: Abstract obtained from the PMC full-text record (PMC12599997; PubMed 41213118; journal version at https://biomedeng.jmir.org/2025/1/e66691) after the DOI landing page returned no content. Accuracy claim about its own system: "the vanilla LLM achieved 17.95% average recall (15.86% weighted), while GAVS achieved 20.63% (18.62% weighted), a statistically significant improvement (P<.001)." Caveat for the audit: the paper is dual-purpose — only the GAVS half is an ICD coder; the GARAG half is guideline-based treatment planning and is out of scope. Also note the paper is industry-authored (Rhazes AI) and evaluates a commercial platform; a preprint of the same work exists under the title "From Challenges to Solutions in Applying Large Language Models to Healthcare..." (preprints.jmir.org/preprint/66691) — same system, same group, so the JMIR version is the fullest and should be the retained record.
screened.adjudicator_reason: Criterion 1 fails: the ICD-10 codes are not assigned to clinical free text about a patient. The paper's own Limitations section states the dataset it used "lacks clinical notes, physical examination findings" — they used the core MIMIC-IV modules, not MIMIC-IV-Note, so no discharge summary, clinic note, radiology/pathology report or doctor's letter was coded. What GPT-4.1 read as "EHR text" is a machine-serialized rendering of structured tables: the Data Availability statement describes "the SQL code used to transform this dataset", the Methods say the evaluation followed Sarvari and Al-Fagih [47], and that paper states verbatim "the MIMIC-IV data did not contain patient history (previous diagnoses and medications), patient physical examinations, and other useful measurements such as electrocardiography (ECG)"; its own source (Health Care Sci 2024;3(1):3-18) describes SQL on BigQuery merging mimiciv_hosp, mimiciv_icu and mimiciv_derived into a text dataframe of microbiology results, intracranial pressures, raw blood gases and min/avg/max aggregates of vitals, blood counts, differentials, cardiac markers, chemistry, coagulation, CRP and enzymes — none of which modules contain narrative notes. The first screener was correct on criteria 2 (GPT-4.1 generation + text-embedding-3-large vector search over the official ICD-10 ontology, explicitly not a supervised classifier), 3 (own-system recall 20.63% vs 17.95%, P<.001, plus explainability claim) and 4 (JMIR Biomedical Engineering Original Paper), but it explicitly noted it could not confirm the note type and defaulted to inclusion; the full text resolves that gap against inclusion. Coding a serialized lab/vital-sign table dump is not coding clinical free text, so the pre-registered rule is not met.

screened.title: Refine Medical Diagnosis Using Generation Augmented Retrieval and Clinical Practice Guidelines
screened.evidence_quote: It (1) integrates LLM predictions with EHR data to create semantically rich queries, (2) retrieves relevant CPG knowledge snippets via embedding similarity, and (3) fuses guideline content with model output to generate clinically aligned recommendations.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM + generation-augmented retrieval (embedding-similarity retrieval over clinical practice guidelines), but it is not used to assign ICD codes — it consumes an upstream model's predictions and outputs guideline-grounded recommendations.
screened.text_type: EHR data plus prior LLM diagnosis predictions used as a query; the retrieved/output text is clinical practice guideline content and recommendations, not an assigned ICD code set.
screened.note: Abstract obtained from the openly available preprint of the same work (arXiv:2506.21615; DOI resolves to IEEE Xplore document 11286217, which is paywalled). The paper explicitly positions itself AGAINST ICD-code-based output: "Current medical language models... typically predict ICD code-based diagnosis from electronic health records (EHRs) because these labels are readily available. However, ICD codes do not capture the nuanced, context-rich reasoning clinicians use for diagnosis." GARMLE-G takes existing model predictions plus EHR data and retrieves guideline snippets to produce evidence-based recommendations (prototype: hypertension diagnosis). Its accuracy claims are about retrieval precision, semantic relevance and guideline adherence versus RAG baselines — not about ICD code assignment. So criterion 1 fails (no ICD codes assigned to clinical free text); it also falls under the exclusion for systems where the LLM works around/queries existing codes rather than assigning them. Criteria 2, 3 and 4 would be satisfied.

screened.title: Leveraging Large Language Models to Extract and Translate Medical Information in Doctors' Notes for Health Records and Diagnostic Billing Codes
screened.criterion: 2 (decisive: coder is an LLM/RAG pipeline, not a supervised encoder); 1, 3 and 4 also satisfied
screened.evidence_quote: The work focuses on using open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract clinical information from physician notes and translate it into ICD-10-CM diagnostic codes without reliance on cloud-based services.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM / RAG — open-weight local LLMs (Llama 3.2, Mistral, Phi, DeepSeek) served via Ollama+LangChain, evaluated under zero-shot, few-shot and retrieval-augmented generation prompting; no supervised encoder/classifier is involved
screened.text_type: Physician (doctors') notes — clinical free-text documentation about a patient; the evaluation corpus is a purpose-built benchmark of SYNTHETIC medical notes rather than real EHR notes
screened.note:
Abstract retrieved from https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22625 (the DOI 302-redirects there). Criterion-by-criterion: (1) target text is physician notes coded to ICD-10-CM — clinical documentation genre, satisfied; (2) coding mechanism is generative open-weight LLMs with zero-shot/few-shot/RAG prompting, explicitly not a supervised encoder — satisfied and decisive; (3) the paper makes accuracy claims about its own system ("strict JSON schema enforcement achieved near 100% formatting compliance, but accurate generation of specific diagnostic codes remains challenging for smaller local models (7B-20B parameters)", few-shot "degraded performance", RAG "reducing overall accuracy") — satisfied, and the claims are negative about its own pipeline, which is still a claim about its own system; (4) full-length work — satisfied.

Two borderline points recorded rather than used to exclude, since the pre-registered rule does not license excluding on either: (a) the notes are SYNTHETIC ("a novel benchmark of synthetic medical notes"), so no real patient text is coded; the rule's non-clinical-text exclusion enumerates genres (drug labels, regulatory documents, death registers, trial descriptions) and synthetic clinical notes are not among them. (b) The document self-describes as a thesis ("this thesis explores an on-device, offline automatic medical coding system") posted to arXiv; theses are not in criterion 4's exclusion list (abstract, poster, editorial, protocol, software deposit, book chapter, front-matter) and this is a full-length work. It also contributes a benchmark, but the benchmark/dataset exclusion does not bite because the study does itself build a coder. If the audit protocol elsewhere restricts to real clinical text or to non-thesis publication types, this record flips to EXCLUDE on (a) or (b) respectively — flagging for the reviewer rather than deciding it unilaterally.
screened.adjudicator_reason: Refutation attempted on all four criteria and failed. (2) Mechanism is unambiguously generative: open-weight LLMs (Llama 3.2, Mistral, Phi, DeepSeek) served via Ollama/LangChain under zero-shot, few-shot and RAG prompting; no supervised encoder/classifier, no training set, and the reported failure modes (few-shot hallucination/overfitting, RAG context-window saturation) are generative-model failure modes. (1) Direction is note -> ICD-10-CM code assignment on physician notes, not code interpretation and not phenotyping; the notes are synthetic rather than real EHR text, but synthetic clinician notes are documents in the clinical-note genre about a (simulated) patient and are not among the rule's enumerated non-clinical text types (drug labels, regulatory documents, death registers, trial descriptions). (3) Explicit accuracy claims about its own system: near-100% JSON schema formatting compliance, specific code generation unreliable at 7B-20B, few-shot degrading performance, RAG reducing overall accuracy. (4) 45-page, 19-figure arXiv preprint (submitted 14 Jan 2026; Hartnett, Huang, Hartnett, Hartnett; cs.IR/cs.CL) that self-describes as a thesis; a thesis is not among the excluded formats (abstract, poster, editorial, protocol, software deposit, book chapter, front-matter) and is full-length. The benchmark-exclusion does not apply because the work itself builds and evaluates a coder. Residual flags for sensitivity analysis, not grounds for exclusion under the rule as written: synthetic rather than real clinical corpus, and unrefereed thesis-preprint status.

screened.title: Accurate Clinical Entity Recognition and Code Mapping of Anatomopathological Reports Using BioClinicalBERT Enhanced by Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Hybrid Deep Learning Approach
screened.criterion: 2 (the deciding criterion; 1, 3 and 4 are also met)
screened.evidence_quote: The entity extraction utilized BioBERT v1.1, while the normalization combined BioClinicalBERT multi-label classification with retrieval-augmented generation, incorporating both dense and BM25 sparse retrieval over SNOMED CT, LOINC, and ICD-11.
screened.coder_mechanism: hybrid — BioClinicalBERT multi-label classifier combined with a retrieval-augmented generation component (dense + BM25 retrieval over SNOMED CT, LOINC, ICD-11); the RAG sits inside the code-assignment step itself, not elsewhere in the paper
screened.text_type: clinical free text about patients — 560 anatomopathological (surgical pathology) reports from the Military Hospital of Tunis, Tunisia
screened.note: Criterion 1: ICD-11 (an ICD revision) is one of three target terminologies, assigned to pathology reports — explicitly a clinical free-text type. Criterion 3: own-system accuracy claims (overall NER F1 0.963, 95% CI 0.933–0.982; ICD-11 macro-F1 0.7201). Criterion 4: full research article in Bioengineering, not an abstract/editorial. Criterion 2 is the borderline one and the reason this is a judgement call: BioClinicalBERT alone would be excluded, but the abstract states the normalization *combined* that classifier *with* retrieval-augmented generation, and that "the combination of BioClinicalBERT and dense retrieval outperformed the standalone and BM25-based approaches" — so the coder is not SOLELY a supervised encoder, and the RAG is part of the coding mechanism rather than an auxiliary use (data generation, acronym expansion). Caveat for the auditor: the abstract names no generative LLM; only the retrieval half of the "RAG" is described concretely, so a full-text check would be worthwhile to confirm a generation component exists. Two other flags for the record: (a) recorded year 2025 matches Crossref (published 27 Dec 2025) even though the DOI is volume 13 issue 1; (b) ICD-11 is one of three ontologies, with SNOMED CT and LOINC being non-ICD targets — ICD coding is a proper subset of what the system does, not its sole aim.
screened.adjudicator_reason: Fails criterion 2. Full text (PMC12838374) verified twice: the coder is BioBERT v1.1 for NER, then a BioClinicalBERT multi-label classification head plus cosine-similarity nearest-neighbour retrieval over BioClinicalBERT-encoded SNOMED CT / LOINC / ICD-11 vectors (FAISS), with BM25 as a sparse comparator, arbitrated by a learned weighted fusion rule. No autoregressive/generative language model appears anywhere in the code-assignment path — no GPT, Llama, Mistral, T5, BART, Gemini or Qwen. The paper's "retrieval-augmented generation" label is a misnomer the authors apply to pure embedding retrieval (they even write "BioClinicalBERT + BM25 (sparse retrieval-augmented generation without dense embeddings)"); nothing is generated, and retrieval here augments a supervised encoder rather than conditioning a generator. The single generative model mentioned is ChatGPT, disclosed only as a manuscript grammar-editing tool — precisely the "LLM used elsewhere in the paper" pattern the rule excludes. The first screener's justification ("the RAG sits inside the code-assignment step itself") conflates retrieval inside the coding step with an LLM/RAG coder; proximity does not satisfy criterion 2. Criteria 1 (560 anatomopathological reports, Military Hospital of Tunis), 3 (ICD-11 macro-F1 0.7201, accuracy 0.8491) and 4 (full MDPI research article) are met, but criterion 2 is decisive and fails, so this is a supervised-classifier coder and ineligible.

screened.title: Augmenting Structured Diagnoses through Effective Use of Pre-trained Large Language Models on Clinical Notes
screened.criterion: 2 (decisive: coder is an LLM, not a supervised encoder); criteria 1, 3 and 4 also satisfied
screened.evidence_quote: We used GPT-OSS for prompt engineering and task segmentation to create a model that extracts ICD-10-CM diagnoses, with estimates of severity, currency, and importance, from progress notes.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM (GPT-OSS, prompt engineering plus task segmentation; no study-specific fine-tuning — "without the need for expensive study-specific model refinement")
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about patients: outpatient provider progress notes (100 notes per cohort, patients aged 0-21; 130 notes expert-reviewed), coded to ICD-10-CM and compared with EHR structured diagnoses
screened.note: Abstract retrieved via the bioRxiv/medRxiv API (https://api.biorxiv.org/details/medrxiv/10.64898/2026.05.30.26354533) after the DOI landing page returned HTTP 403; medRxiv v1, posted 2026-06-02, category "health informatics". Criterion 1 met: ICD-10-CM assigned to progress notes. Criterion 3 met: explicit accuracy claims about its own system — "Compared to expert review, LLM precision was 0.84 and recall 0.49 for exact matches, and 0.92 and 0.62, respectively, for category-level matching." Criterion 4 met: full structured preprint (Objective/Methods/Results/Conclusion), not a conference abstract, poster, editorial, protocol, or software deposit. No exclusion applies — the output is an assigned ICD code set per note, not a patient-level phenotype label, and the paper builds its own coder rather than reporting a benchmark or review. Not a duplicate of any other record seen in this screen.
screened.adjudicator_reason: Read the full abstract independently via Europe PMC (PPR1244161; medRxiv preprint, 2026-06-02) after medRxiv/ResearchGate returned 403. All four criteria hold and every refutation angle failed. (1) Clinical free text about patients: outpatient provider progress notes for patients aged 0-21, coded to ICD-10-CM. (2) Mechanism is a generative LLM, not a supervised encoder: GPT-OSS driven by prompt engineering and task segmentation, explicitly with no study-specific fine-tuning ("without the need for expensive study-specific model refinement"); no BERT/RoBERTa-family classifier appears anywhere in the pipeline. (3) Accuracy claims about its own system: precision 0.84 / recall 0.49 exact, 0.92 / 0.62 at category level versus expert review, plus 18.7% exact and 33.3% category agreement with EHR codes and 0.93 semantic similarity. (4) Full preprint with structured Objective/Methods/Results/Conclusion — not an abstract, poster, editorial, protocol, or software deposit; preprints are not an excluded publication type. Exclusion checks: the "multiple cohorts" are sampling strata, not the output — the output unit is a per-note ICD-10-CM code set, so this is code assignment, not phenotyping; direction is note-to-code, not code interpretation or code-description generation; the paper builds and evaluates its own coder rather than merely offering a benchmark; no evidence of a fuller duplicate report by the same group.

screened.title: Enhancing Clinical Note Generation with ICD-10, Clinical Ontology Knowledge Graphs, and Chain-of-Thought Prompting Using GPT-4
screened.criterion: Criterion 1 (fails) — plus the named exclusion for studies where an LLM uses/interprets existing codes rather than assigning codes to a note
screened.evidence_quote: In our prompts, we use as input International Classification of Diseases codes and basic patient information.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM (GPT-4 with Chain-of-Thought prompting, semantic search, and a clinical-ontology knowledge graph) — but it is a note GENERATOR, not a coder; no ICD code assignment is performed
screened.text_type: None coded. The system runs in the inverse direction: ICD-10 codes plus basic patient information are the INPUT, and free-text clinical notes are the OUTPUT (evaluated on six clinical cases from the CodiEsp test set).
screened.note: Abstract retrieved via Crossref API for DOI 10.1177/15578666251411390 (Journal of Computational Biology, 2026). Direction of the task is decisive: the pipeline consumes ICD codes and produces clinical notes ("We investigate the usage of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt engineering to improve the LLM's response in clinical note generation"), so criterion 1 (assigning ICD codes to clinical free text about a patient) is not met. It also matches the explicit exclusion for LLMs that interpret or consume existing codes rather than assigning them. Criteria 2 (LLM mechanism), 3 (accuracy claim about its own system — "our results show that it outperformed the clinical notes generated by standard one-shot prompts"), and 4 (full journal paper) are satisfied, but criterion 1 fails and all four are required. Note the CodiEsp dataset is normally an ICD-coding benchmark; here it is repurposed as a source of cases for generation, not for code assignment. No speculation beyond the abstract text was used.

screened.title: Zero-Shot ATC Coding with Large Language Models for Clinical Assessments
screened.criterion: Fails criterion 1 (no ICD codes assigned); triggers the named exclusion "non-ICD terminologies as the target (e.g. ATC drug codes)"
screened.evidence_quote: Manual assignment of Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) codes to prescription records is a significant bottleneck in healthcare research and operations at Ontario Health and InterRAI Canada, requiring extensive expert time and effort.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM (zero-shot GPT-4o and open-source Llama 3.1 70B/8B, plus a fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B, prompted hierarchically level-by-level through the ATC ontology)
screened.text_type: Prescription/drug records — Health Canada drug product data, the RABBITS benchmark, and clinical notes from Ontario Health — but the assignment target is ATC drug codes, not ICD codes
screened.note: Abstract retrieved from https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07743. The system is genuinely LLM-based (satisfying criterion 2) and makes an accuracy claim about itself, 78% exact match with GPT-4o and 60% with Llama 3.1 70B (satisfying criterion 3), and it does touch real clinical notes. It is nevertheless excluded because the target terminology is ATC, not ICD: the abstract states only that the method was "Inspired by recent advances in automatic International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding," which is framing, not ICD assignment. This falls squarely under the pre-registered exclusion for non-ICD terminologies. Note: several web/MCP tool calls initially failed with a transient classifier-availability error before the fetch succeeded; the abstract quoted here is the verbatim arXiv abstract.

screened.title: MAX-EVAL-11: A Large Scale Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Full-Spectrum ICD-11 Medical Coding
screened.criterion: Named exclusion: "BENCHMARKS/DATASETS that do not themselves build a coder" (also fails criterion 3 — no accuracy or explainability claim about its OWN coding system; the accuracy claims are about third-party off-the-shelf LLMs measured on the new benchmark)
screened.evidence_quote: We introduce MAX-EVAL-11, the first large-scale benchmark for full-spectrum ICD-11 medical coding.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM (off-the-shelf, evaluated not built) — the paper benchmarks state-of-the-art general-purpose LLMs (best: Claude 4 Sonnet, weighted score 0.433) plus a specialized medical model (MedCoder); it contributes a dataset and a hierarchical scoring framework, not a coding system of its own
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about patients — 10,000 MIMIC-III discharge summaries with mapped, expert-validated ICD-11 annotations (criterion 1 is satisfied; the exclusion is on the benchmark/system axis, not the text axis)
screened.note: Abstract retrieved from https://aclanthology.org/2026.bionlp-1.23 (DOI 10.18653/v1/2026.bionlp-1.23 302-redirects there). Authors: Ujjwal Singh, Sarthak Deshwal, Nitish Dube, Arjun Sharma; BioNLP 2026, San Diego. Criteria 1 and 4 are met (clinical discharge summaries; full paper), but the record fails the explicit benchmark/dataset exclusion: the contribution is the benchmark (10,000 annotated summaries) plus a hierarchical partial-credit evaluation framework, and every accuracy figure reported (weighted score 0.433, exact-match 0–4.8%) characterizes externally developed models rather than a coder the authors built. Also noted: a near-duplicate preprint of the same work exists on medRxiv under the title "MAX-EVAL-11: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Full-Spectrum ICD-11 Medical Coding" (DOI 10.1101/2025.10.30.25339130); the medRxiv landing page returned HTTP 403, but its indexed summary matches this abstract (same 10,000 MIMIC-III notes, same Claude 4 Sonnet 0.433 figure). If that preprint appears as a separate record in the audit it should be excluded on the same grounds and additionally as a duplicate report of the same work — the BioNLP version is the fuller one.

screened.title: MedicalBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Toward Improved Medical Concept Extraction
screened.criterion: Named exclusion — "BENCHMARKS/DATASETS that do not themselves build a coder"; also fails criterion 3 (no accuracy/explainability claim about its own coding system) and criterion 1 (task is verification of given note-concept pairs, not assignment of codes to a note).
screened.evidence_quote: We present MedicalBench, a benchmark for medical concept extraction with evidence grounding that evaluates implicit medical reasoning.
screened.coder_mechanism: No coder is built. The paper releases a benchmark and evaluates off-the-shelf third-party LLMs on it ("Benchmarking state-of-the-art LLMs reveals that performance remains modest"). An LLM appears only as (a) a multi-stage triage pipeline used to curate the dataset and (b) the systems under test — neither is a coder the authors propose.
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about patients — MIMIC-IV discharge summaries paired with human-verified ICD-10 codes. The text type would satisfy criterion 1, but the formulated task is binary verification over note-concept pairs plus sentence-level evidence retrieval, not assignment of an ICD code set to a note.
screened.note: Abstract retrieved from https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20197v1 (the bare /abs/ URL and the doi.org landing page were not reachable during the session; the v1 page resolved). Clean-cut benchmark exclusion: the contribution is a dataset and evaluation protocol ("MedicalBench formulates medical concept extraction as a verification task over medical note-concept pairs, coupled with sentence-level evidence identification"), and the accuracy/interpretability claims are about other people's LLMs measured on that benchmark, not about a system the authors built. Note the ICD-10 codes are inputs/labels used to construct the note-concept pairs, so the LLMs judge whether a supplied concept holds rather than producing a code assignment. Borderline only in that the explainability framing ("assessment of both correctness and interpretability") superficially resembles criterion 3; it does not survive because there is no own system.

screened.title: Large language models are good medical coders, if provided with tools
screened.criterion: 1 (clinical free text about a patient) — fails; input is isolated single-term condition names, not clinical documentation
screened.evidence_quote: Evaluating both systems on a dataset of 100 single-term medical conditions, the Retrieve-Rank system achieved 100% accuracy in predicting correct ICD-10-CM codes, significantly outperforming the Vanilla LLM (GPT-3.5-turbo), which achieved only 6% accuracy.
screened.coder_mechanism: RAG pipeline — a two-stage Retrieve-Rank system (retrieval over the ICD-10-CM vocabulary followed by LLM reranking), compared against a vanilla GPT-3.5-turbo baseline. Criterion 2 would be satisfied.
screened.text_type: Isolated single-term medical condition names (a 100-item term list), not patient-level clinical free text such as discharge summaries, clinic notes, or reports. The paper itself flags "the limitations of using simplified inputs and the need for further testing on more complex, realistic medical cases."
screened.note: Abstract obtained from the arXiv /abs/ page (arXiv:2407.12849, Keith Kwan, submitted July 2024; 7 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables — a full preprint, so criterion 4 is met, and the 100%-vs-6% accuracy claim about its own system satisfies criterion 3). Exclusion rests solely on criterion 1: the system maps a bare condition term to an ICD-10-CM code rather than assigning codes to a patient note. This is effectively terminology lookup / code-description matching, which the pre-registered rule also names under the explicit exclusion for LLMs that "interpret or query existing codes rather than assigning codes to a note." No evidence in the abstract of evaluation on any clinical document; the authors explicitly defer realistic clinical cases to future work. Decision is unambiguous and does not depend on ambiguous reading.

screened.title: Autonomous International Classification of Diseases Coding Using Pretrained Language Models and Advanced Prompt Learning Techniques: Evaluation of an Automated Analysis System Using Medical Text
screened.evidence_quote: We integrated 4 components into our framework: a medical pretrained BERT, a keyword filtration BERT in a functional order, a fine-tuning phase, and task-specific prompt learning utilizing mixed templates and soft verbalizers.
screened.coder_mechanism: supervised encoder — a fine-tuned medical pretrained BERT ("Key-BERT") pipeline with a second keyword-filtration BERT and prompt learning (mixed templates + soft verbalizers) over the masked-LM head; no generative LLM and no retrieval-augmented generation. Baselines are RoBERTa, XLNet, and other BERT fine-tuning pipelines, confirming the encoder-classifier family.
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about patients — long free-text medical records / narratives from a multicenter dataset (584,969 records), coded to ICD-10 for 13 common cardiovascular diseases.
screened.note: Resolved via Crossref then PubMed/EFetch; full verbatim abstract read. Record metadata says 2024/venue unknown; actual publication is JMIR Medical Informatics 2025;13:e63020 (PMID 39761555, e-published Jan 2025) — a full original research paper. Criteria 1, 3 and 4 are satisfied: it assigns ICD-10 codes to clinical free text about patients, it makes an accuracy claim about its own system ("our approach achieved a higher micro-F1-score of 0.838 and a macro-area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (macro-AUC) of 0.958"), and it is a full journal article. It fails ONLY criterion 2. The title phrase "pretrained language models" and the use of "prompt learning" could be mistaken for LLM prompting, but the abstract makes clear the prompting is soft-template/soft-verbalizer tuning on a fine-tuned BERT encoder, which the pre-registered rule explicitly rules out ("A BERT/RoBERTa/BioClinicalBERT classifier is NOT eligible"). No LLM or retrieval component is described anywhere in the abstract.

screened.title: Leveraging Language Models for Inpatient Diagnosis Coding
screened.criterion: 2 (coding mechanism must be an LLM or RAG pipeline, not solely a supervised encoder/classifier)
screened.evidence_quote: A total of three language models, including two general-purpose and a domain-specific model, were evaluated and compared. The results show competitive performance among the models, with the domain-specific model achieving the highest micro-averaged F1 score of 0.7821 and mean average precision of 0.8097.
screened.coder_mechanism: supervised encoder — fine-tuned transformer encoders used as multi-label ICD-10 classifiers (the "domain-specific model" is MEDPSU-RoBERTa, a RoBERTa-architecture model pre-trained on ~80M institutional clinical documents; the general-purpose comparators are multilingual BERT and multilingual E5). No generative LLM and no retrieval-augmented generation is used to assign codes.
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about patients — inpatient admission documentation from a single hospital (230,645 admissions, six years), coded to the full ICD-10 code set (8,677 codes). Criterion 1 is satisfied; the failure is on mechanism.
screened.note: Record had no DOI recorded; resolved by exact-title search to Suvirat K., Tanasanchonnakul D., Chairat S., Chaichulee S., Applied Sciences 13(16):9450, 2023 (MDPI, open access; ProQuest docview 2856801154). Abstract obtained via the OpenAlex record (abstract_inverted_index reconstruction) and cross-checked against an independent abstract mirror (ouci.dntb.gov.ua/en/works/40ymqBpl/); the MDPI landing page and PDF both returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch. Criteria 1, 3 (accuracy claims about its own system: micro-F1 0.7821, mAP 0.8097) and 4 (full journal paper) all hold, but criterion 2 fails: the abstract's "language models" are encoder-only models fine-tuned as supervised multi-label classifiers, which the pre-registered rule explicitly rules out ("A BERT/RoBERTa/BioClinicalBERT classifier is NOT eligible"). The micro-averaged F1 / mean-average-precision framing over an 8,677-label space is itself the signature of multi-label classification rather than generation. Nothing in the abstract or the retrievable body text indicates generative or retrieval-augmented code assignment. Judgement is confident; the only residual uncertainty is that the decisive model names come from the paper body rather than the abstract sentence quoted above, which on its own says only "three language models".

screened.title: Evaluating the Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language Models for Medical Coding and Hospital Readmission Risk Stratification: Zero-Shot Prompting Approach
screened.criterion: 2 (decisive: coding mechanism is a prompted LLM, not a supervised encoder); criteria 1, 3 and 4 also satisfied
screened.evidence_quote: Using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV dataset, we selected a random cohort of 300 hospital discharge summaries. Prompts were engineered to include structured clinical content from 5 note sections: chief complaints, past medical history, surgical history, laboratories, and imaging. Prompts were standardized and zero-shot, with no model fine-tuning or repetition across runs.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM — general-purpose models (ChatGPT-4, LLaMA-3.1, Gemini-1.5, DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI-O3) prompted zero-shot through public web UIs, with rationale elicitation; no fine-tuning, no supervised encoder, no retrieval component
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about a patient: 300 hospital discharge summaries from MIMIC-IV (chief complaint, past medical history, surgical history, labs, imaging sections)
screened.note: Full title recorded in the record ("Evaluating the Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language Models for Medical Coding") is a truncation of the JMIR 2025;27:e74142 original paper (PMID 40737604, PMC12310144); published as a peer-reviewed Original Paper, so criterion 4 holds. Criterion 1: ICD-9 codes assigned to MIMIC-IV discharge summaries (one of three tasks; the other two — primary diagnosis generation and readmission risk stratification — do not disqualify the paper because the ICD-9 task is present). Criterion 3: explicit accuracy claims about its own prompting setup (ICD-9 correctness: LLaMA-3.1 42.6%, ChatGPT-4 40.6%, Gemini-1.5 14.6%, OpenAI-O3 45.3%; F1-scores) plus an explainability claim ("Despite improved explainability, reasoning models generated verbose responses"; "Reasoning models offer marginally better performance and increased interpretability"). Considered and rejected the "benchmark that does not itself build a coder" exclusion: the authors construct and evaluate their own zero-shot prompting pipeline (engineered section-structured prompts + rationale elicitation) that emits ICD-9 codes, rather than releasing a dataset/benchmark. Duplicate note: an SSRN preprint of the same work exists (Naliyatthaliyazchayil, Muthyala, Purkayastha, Gichoya; SSRN abstract_id=5172464) — the JMIR version is the fullest and should be the retained record. Abstract text verified independently from two sources (PubMed and PMC) with identical wording.
screened.adjudicator_reason: Refutation attempted on all three standard failure modes and none succeeded. (1) Mechanism: ICD-9 codes are assigned by zero-shot prompted general-purpose LLMs (ChatGPT-4, LLaMA-3.1, Gemini-1.5, DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI-O3) with no fine-tuning. The paper does use SciBERT (allenai/scibert_scivocab_uncased via SentenceTransformer, cosine threshold >=0.7), but only to score diagnosis-string similarity during evaluation; it never assigns codes, so this is not a supervised-encoder coder. Criterion 2 holds. (2) Text: 300 deidentified MIMIC-IV hospital discharge summaries, with free-text sections (chief complaint, past medical history, surgical history, labs, imaging) fed to the models; the models emit ICD-9 codes scored against MIMIC ground truth, i.e. genuine code assignment, not code-to-name interpretation. The paper's third task (readmission risk) is patient-label prediction, but it is a separate task and does not negate the coding task. Criterion 1 holds. (3) Not an excluded benchmark/dataset: the authors build their own prompting pipeline and report accuracy for it (ICD-9 correctness 14.6% Gemini-1.5 to 45.3% OpenAI-O3), plus reasoning/interpretability claims. Criterion 3 holds. (4) Full-length JMIR Original Paper, 2025;27:e74142, peer-reviewed, not an abstract or letter. Criterion 4 holds. Minor non-disqualifying caveat: input is a programmatically assembled section template with the primary diagnosis withheld rather than the raw whole note, which limits comparability of the accuracy figures to full-note coders.

screened.title: Automated ICD-O-3 Coding of Real-World Pathology Reports Using Self-Hosted Large Language Models
screened.criterion: All four met; criterion 2 (LLM coding mechanism) is decisive, with criterion 1 satisfied by ICD-O-3 assignment to pathology reports and criterion 3 by reported F1 scores.
screened.evidence_quote: To evaluate the performance of multiple state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) in extracting ICD-O-3 topography and morphology codes from real-world pathology reports and assess their potential for clinical implementation, this study compares the performance of state-of-the-art open-source models in multiple evaluation setups.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM (prompted self-hosted open-weight LLMs: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama 8B/70B, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Gemma-3-12B-it; three task-specific prompts, no supervised encoder classifier)
screened.text_type: Real-world clinical pathology reports about patients (21,364 reports from 10,823 patients, 2013-2025, large German hospital)
screened.resolved_doi: 10.1200/CCI-25-00254 (journal version, JCO Clinical Cancer Informatics; preprint: 10.1101/2025.07.23.25332040)
screened.note: Abstract retrieved via Europe PMC (PMID 41812101); medRxiv landing page returned HTTP 403. Criterion 1: ICD-O-3 is an ICD revision (International Classification of Diseases for Oncology) assigned to clinical free text - not a non-ICD terminology and not phenotyping, since the output is an assigned code set per report. Criterion 2: coding is done purely by prompting self-hosted LLMs; no supervised encoder/classifier is the coder. Criterion 3: explicit accuracy claims about their own setup ("Qwen3-235B-A22B achieved the highest performance (microaverage F1: 71.6%)"; morphology exact microaverage F1 34.7%). Criterion 4: full Journal Article (Europe PMC pubType "Journal Article"), not an abstract or poster. Not an excluded benchmark/dataset paper: the authors build and deploy the coding pipeline (prompt design, hospital infrastructure) and evaluate it on their own institutional data. Duplicate handling: this record (2025 medRxiv preprint) and the 2026 JCO CCI article "Automated Tumor International Classification of Diseases Coding of Real-World Pathology Reports Using Self-Hosted Large Language Models" are the same system by the same group (Arzideh et al., University Hospital Essen) - keep the fuller journal version (10.1200/CCI-25-00254) and drop the preprint if both are in the pool. Caveat noted for the audit: the paper is a comparison across five off-the-shelf models rather than a single novel architecture, but it still assigns codes and claims accuracy, so it passes the pre-registered rule as written.

screened.title: Large Language Models for Automated ICD-10 Coding of Obstetric Clinical Notes in Portuguese: Comparison With Human Coders
screened.criterion: 2 (all four hold; criterion 2 is the decisive one — the coder is a prompted/fine-tuned general-purpose LLM, not a supervised encoder)
screened.evidence_quote: We benchmarked six general-purpose LLMs for hierarchical ICD-10 coding of 1,117 obstetric discharge summaries written in Brazilian Portuguese.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM — six general-purpose LLMs prompted for hierarchical ICD-10 code assignment (best: GPT-4o), plus a lightweight supervised fine-tuning variant on code–description pairs and a Portuguese-to-English translation condition. No supervised encoder/classifier (BERT-family) is the coder.
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about patients: 1,117 obstetric discharge summaries written in Brazilian Portuguese.
screened.note: Abstract obtained from Europe PMC REST (record PPR1151504) after researchsquare.com and researchgate.net both returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch; Crossref independently confirms the DOI and title. Criterion 1 satisfied (obstetric discharge summaries = clinical documentation about a patient). Criterion 2 satisfied (LLMs are the coding mechanism). Criterion 3 satisfied — explicit accuracy claims about its own runs: "Even the best-performing model (GPT-4o) achieved only modest agreement with the human reference, with micro-F1 scores of 0.36 at the three-character level and 0.15 at the leaf level," and "human-coded references achieved a precision of 0.77, compared to 0.59 for the strongest model." A negative accuracy claim is still an accuracy claim about the authors' own system. Criterion 4 satisfied: this is a full structured preprint (Background/Methods/Results/Conclusions) on Research Square, indexed by Europe PMC as pubType "Preprint" — not a conference abstract, poster, editorial, protocol, software deposit, book chapter, or front-matter; the pre-registered rule does not exclude preprints. Borderline considered and rejected: the word "benchmarked" invites the BENCHMARK/DATASET exclusion, but that exclusion targets benchmarks that "do not themselves build a coder." Here the authors construct and run the coding pipelines (prompting, translation, and supervised fine-tuning) on their own institutional corpus and report accuracy of those pipelines, so the coder is built rather than merely leaderboarded. Note for the audit: venue is a non-peer-reviewed preprint and year is recorded as 2026; flag if the protocol restricts to peer-reviewed publications, and check for a later journal version to avoid a duplicate-report conflict.
screened.adjudicator_reason: Refutation attempted and failed on all four criteria. (1) Clinical free text about patients: 1,117 obstetric discharge summaries, an explicitly named eligible document type. (2) Mechanism: the coder is six prompted general-purpose LLMs (GPT-4o best) plus a fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini variant and a Portuguese-to-English translation condition; no BERT-family supervised encoder is used as the coder anywhere, so the commonest error (encoder mislabeled as LLM pipeline) does not apply. (3) Accuracy claim about its own system: micro-F1 0.36 category / 0.15 leaf, precision 0.59 vs 0.77 for human coders. (4) Full Research Square preprint (Crossref type posted-content), not an abstract, poster, editorial, protocol, or front matter. The strongest counter-argument — that the word "benchmarked" triggers the BENCHMARKS/DATASETS exclusion — fails because that exclusion covers resource papers that build no coder, whereas these authors construct a hierarchical category-to-leaf prompting pipeline and a fine-tuned model and report its own accuracy on real patient notes. A secondary objection, that fine-tuning on code-description pairs is code interpretation rather than assignment, also fails: those pairs are training data, while the evaluated task is assigning codes to discharge summaries. Negative results (LLMs below human reliability) are not an exclusion ground under the pre-registered rule. No duplicate version by the same group was found.

screened.title: An automated information extraction model for unstructured discharge letters using large language models and GPT-4
screened.criterion: All four hold; criterion 1 and 2 are the pivotal ones (ICD-10 codes assigned to discharge letters by GPT-4), with 3 satisfied by the reported accuracies and 4 by full-article status in Healthcare Analytics vol. 7 (2025), art. 100378.
screened.evidence_quote: The International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10) codes for the identified diagnoses achieved an accuracy of 85% for primary diagnoses and 60.7% for secondary diagnoses.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM — GPT-4 (OpenAI) driven by a standardized, then fine-tuned, extraction prompt; open-source LLMs tested as comparators. No supervised encoder/classifier, no retrieval component described.
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about patients: unstructured German discharge letters (ten patients from each of two German healthcare institutions).
screened.note: Record title was truncated ("...using large language models"); the published title ends "...and GPT-4". Resolved via exact-title web search to the Healthcare Analytics article; abstract read verbatim from the authors' institutional record page (mml.ikim.nrw) since ScienceDirect returned 403. The paper also assigns ATC drug codes, but ICD-10 assignment to clinical notes is an explicit target and outcome, so the "non-ICD terminology as the target" exclusion does not apply. Caveat for the audit, not eligibility: the evaluation set is very small (20 discharge letters total).
screened.adjudicator_reason: Refutation attempted and failed on all four criteria; I verified the abstract verbatim via the authors' institutional publication page (mml.ikim.nrw) after Elsevier returned 403 and the OA PDF timed out. (1) Clinical free text about patients: unstructured German discharge letters for 20 real patients from two German healthcare institutions. (2) Mechanism is purely generative-LLM prompting: GPT-4 driven by a standardized then prompt-fine-tuned extraction template, with open-source LLMs as the only comparators. The commonest error mode does not apply here — there is no BERT/RoBERTa/BioClinicalBERT or any supervised encoder-classifier anywhere in the paper; the word "fine-tuned" in the abstract refers explicitly to the PROMPT ("the prompt was fine-tuned in a second experiment"), not to model weights. (3) Accuracy claim about its own system: 85% (primary) and 60.7% (secondary) ICD-10 accuracy, plus 85%/55.8% diagnosis extraction rising to 95%/88.9% after prompt refinement. (4) Full research article, Healthcare Analytics vol. 7 (2025), art. 100378, with two designed experiments and a comparator arm — not an abstract, poster, or editorial. The second common error mode also does not apply: the direction is text-to-code (letter to ICD-10), not code-to-name generation or code-description benchmarking, and the output is an assigned ICD code set rather than a patient-level phenotype label. Three candidate refutations were considered and rejected: (a) that ICD coding is only a sub-task of a broader information-extraction paper — the rule imposes no primary-task requirement and the ICD-10 sub-task is separately quantified in the abstract; (b) that ATC drug codes trigger the non-ICD-terminology exclusion — ATC is coded IN ADDITION to ICD-10, not instead of it; (c) that a two-stage extract-then-code design means codes are assigned to extracted diagnosis strings rather than to the note — the pipeline input remains the unstructured discharge letter, and extract-then-code is a standard LLM coder architecture. Residual uncertainty: I could not confirm from primary full text whether GPT-4 emits the ICD-10 string directly within its output template or via a mapping step, but the title, the placement of ICD-10 accuracy alongside the other GPT-4 template fields, and the LLM-only comparator set make a non-LLM coder implausible and do not meet the bar to overturn.

screened.title: Large language models vs human for classifying clinical documents
screened.criterion: 2 (decisive); 1, 3 and 4 also satisfied
screened.evidence_quote: We evaluated the performance of ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4 in classifying ICD-10 codes from discharge summaries within selected records of the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC) IV dataset.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM — ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4 prompted directly with a classification prompt; no retrieval and no supervised encoder does the assigning (prior ML/SNOMED-mapping methods are only used upstream to select the 802 hard false-negative cases, and human coders serve as the comparator)
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about patients — discharge summaries from MIMIC-IV, coded to ICD-10
screened.note: Resolved via web search (no DOI in record) to PubMed 39848078; full paper in International Journal of Medical Informatics (2025), Elsevier, ScienceDirect S1386505625000176. Criterion 1: ICD-10 assigned to discharge summaries. Criterion 2: the coder is a general-purpose LLM prompted zero/few-shot, not a supervised classifier — this is the decisive test and it passes. Criterion 3: explicit accuracy and consistency claims about its own system ("ChatGPT 4 demonstrated significantly improved consistency over ChatGPT 3.5, with matching results between runs ranging from 86% to 89% ... ChatGPT matched the median performance of human coders, achieving an accuracy rate of 22%"). Criterion 4: peer-reviewed journal article with Background/Objective/Methods/Results/Conclusion, not an abstract or poster. Caveat worth carrying into extraction: the sample is deliberately adversarial (802 summaries that both ML and SNOMED mapping got wrong), so the 22% accuracy is not comparable to full-corpus MIMIC micro-F1 figures from other included studies; it is a hard-case subset benchmarked against human coders. Not excluded as a benchmark/dataset paper because it does deploy and evaluate its own prompted coding pipeline rather than merely releasing data.
screened.adjudicator_reason: Refutation attempted on the full text (Int J Med Inform 195:105800, open access) and failed. (2) The coder is the LLM itself: ChatGPT 3.5/4 are prompted zero-shot with the raw discharge summary and their yes/no answer is the code decision; the Random Forest (cTAKES features) and SNOMED->ICD-10 mapping are upstream baselines used only to isolate the 802 cases both missed, and never assign the LLM's codes. No supervised encoder is being mislabelled as an LLM pipeline. (1) Text coded is clinical free text about patients — MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, presented unmodified, coded to ICD-10 (A41, I13, I21, I25, Z51). The strongest overturn angle is that the task is binary confirmation of one pre-specified level-3 code rather than open code-set generation, which superficially resembles the phenotyping exclusion; it fails because the label's semantics is the ICD-10 code in the MIMIC-IV record, the paper is framed throughout as clinical coding / CDI / computer-assisted coding, and the comparator is five human clinical coders given the identical prompt. The note is the object being coded, so the 'LLM interprets/queries existing codes' exclusion also does not apply. (3) Explicit accuracy and explainability claims about its own system: 22% overall accuracy for ChatGPT 4 (6.25% A41; 25% I13/I21/I25; 35.71% Z51), run-to-run consistency 86-89% vs 57-67% for 3.5, with a required rationale accompanying each yes/no. (4) Full CC-BY research article with structured abstract, figures, tables and references — not an abstract, poster or editorial. Duplication checked: the same group's 'Can Reasoning LLMs Enhance Clinical Document Classification?' (Health and Technology / arXiv 2504.08040) evaluates eight different reasoning and non-reasoning models with no human-coder arm, so it is a different system, not a duplicate report of this one.

screened.title: Large Language Model in Medical Informatics: Direct Classification and Enhanced Text Representations for Automatic ICD Coding
screened.criterion: All four hold; criterion 2 is the decisive one (LLaMA is applied directly as the classifier, not solely a supervised encoder)
screened.evidence_quote: This paper explores the use of Large Language Models (LLM), specifically the LLAMA architecture, to enhance ICD code classification through two methodologies: direct application as a classifier and as a generator of enriched text representations within a Multi-Filter Residual Convolutional Neural Network (MultiResCNN) framework.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM (LLaMA-2) — two configurations: (a) LLaMA applied directly as the ICD classifier, (b) hybrid, where raw LLaMA-2 embeddings replace the input representations of a MultiResCNN classifier. Configuration (a) alone satisfies criterion 2; the paper is not solely a supervised encoder.
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about a patient — medical discharge summaries (MIMIC-style), coded with ICD codes.
screened.resolved_doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2411.06823 (arXiv:2411.06823); also published as an IEEE conference paper, IEEE Xplore document 10822419
screened.note: Abstract obtained from https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.06823 (authors: Zeyd Boukhers, AmeerAli Khan, Qusai Ramadan, Cong Yang; 2024). Criterion 1 met: ICD codes assigned to discharge summaries. Criterion 2 met: the coder is an LLM (LLaMA), used directly as a classifier — this is not a BERT/RoBERTa supervised-encoder paper, and the LLM is the coding mechanism rather than an auxiliary component. Criterion 3 met: explicit accuracy claim about its own system — "We evaluate these methods by comparing them against state-of-the-art approaches, revealing LLAMA's potential to significantly improve classification outcomes." Criterion 4 met: full IEEE conference paper (arXiv preprint of the same work), not an abstract, poster, or editorial. None of the named exclusions apply: it builds a coder rather than a benchmark/dataset, codes clinical notes rather than non-clinical text, targets ICD rather than another terminology, and outputs an assigned code set rather than a phenotype label. Duplicate-report caveat for the audit: the arXiv preprint and the IEEE Xplore version (doc 10822419) are the same system by the same group — keep the IEEE published version as the fullest record and do not count both. Exact IEEE 10.1109 DOI suffix could not be confirmed (IEEE Xplore landing page not fetchable); the arXiv DOI is verified.
screened.adjudicator_reason: Criteria 1, 3 and 4 hold (MIMIC-III de-identified discharge summaries; own-system accuracy claims in Table I with F1/AUC/P@k; a full ~5-page IEEE conference paper with methods, experiments and references — not an abstract). Criterion 2 fails. The first screener read the abstract phrase "direct application as a classifier" as generative LLM coding, but Section III.A of the paper defines that arm (LLAMA2-C) as LLaMA-2 fine-tuned with a randomly initialised classification head, a softmax over a closed label space (50 or 8239/4216 classes) and cross-entropy loss. There is no prompting, no generation of code strings, and no retrieval — the model emits class indices, not codes. The authors themselves state they are evaluating LLaMA "beyond typical generative uses," explicitly disclaiming the generative mechanism. Architecturally this is identical to a BERT/RoBERTa classifier with a larger backbone: swap the weights and nothing else in the pipeline changes. The second arm (LLAMA2-R+MRCNN) is even further from eligibility — frozen raw LLaMA-2 embeddings are fed to a supervised MultiResCNN that does the actual coding, i.e. the LLM is a feature generator "used elsewhere," directly analogous to the rule's excluded case of an LLM used to produce training inputs. Since both configurations are supervised discriminative classifiers, the paper is *solely* a supervised encoder/classifier study, which criterion 2 excludes. I note the residual tension for the adjudicator: LLaMA-2-7B is indisputably a large language model, and the rule's exclusion examples name only encoder-only BERT variants, so a model-identity reading of criterion 2 would include this paper. But the rule's operative contrast is mechanism ("NOT solely a supervised encoder/classifier"), and the screening instruction directs defaulting to overturn when the mechanism is not clearly an LLM/RAG assigning codes. Here the mechanism is unambiguously supervised multi-label classification, so EXCLUDE.

screened.title: Decoding substance use disorder severity from clinical notes using a large language model
screened.evidence_quote: This study investigates the application of LLMs for extracting severity-related information for various SUD diagnoses from clinical notes.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM — zero-shot prompting of Flan-T5 (Flan-T5-XXL) with crafted prompts and post-processing, benchmarked against a rule-based approach
screened.text_type: Clinical free text about patients (clinical notes containing supplemental unstructured DSM-5 detail)
screened.note: Criteria 2, 3 and 4 are met (LLM coder, accuracy/recall claim about its own system, full paper in npj Mental Health Research 2025). Criterion 1 fails: the system does not assign ICD codes. Its output is a DSM-5 severity specifier (mild/moderate/severe, plus remission status) attached to 11 SUD diagnosis categories. The abstract explicitly frames ICD-10 as the thing that is INSUFFICIENT — "Existing diagnostic coding systems used by insurance providers, like the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10), lack granularity for certain diagnoses, but American clinicians will add this granularity (as that found within the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders classification or DSM-5) as supplemental unstructured text in clinical notes." ICD-10 is therefore the baseline being supplemented, not the target terminology being assigned. The extracted severity label is a patient/diagnosis attribute rather than an assigned ICD code set, which also matches the pre-registered exclusion for outputs that are patient labels rather than ICD codes. Note the record's year field (2025) matches the journal issue; the DOI stem is 2024.

screened.title: Coding Historical Causes of Death Data with Large Language Models
screened.criterion: Criterion 1 fails — named exclusion: "coding of NON-clinical text (… historical death registers)"
screened.evidence_quote: We evaluate the ability of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Llama 2 LLMs to accurately assign ICD-10 codes on the HiCaD dataset that contains causes of death recorded in the civil death register entries of 19,361 individuals from Ipswich, Kilmarnock, and the Isle of Skye from the UK between 1861-1901.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM (prompted generative models: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2), compared against standard supervised ML baselines
screened.text_type: Short historical cause-of-death strings transcribed from 19th-century UK civil death register entries (1861-1901) — not clinical documentation about a patient
screened.note: Criteria 2 and 3 are satisfied — the coder is genuinely an LLM (zero/few-shot GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2, not a supervised encoder) and the paper makes accuracy claims about its own system (69%/83%/40% correct-code rates vs 89% for standard ML). It fails on the text being coded: the input is archival civil death register cause-of-death text, which the protocol explicitly names as non-clinical ("historical death registers"), and it is not documentation authored about a patient's care. Secondary note: the published venue is a Springer LNCS proceedings chapter (AISoLA 2024, "Bridging the Gap Between AI and Reality"), which is a full paper, so criterion 4 is not the reason for exclusion. Abstract retrieved verbatim from the arXiv /abs page.

screened.title: Evaluating Enhanced LLMs for Precise Mental Health Diagnosis from Clinical Notes
screened.criterion: All four hold; criterion 1 and 2 are decisive (ICD-10-CM codes assigned to psychiatric clinical notes by RAG-enhanced LLMs), criterion 3 satisfied by the reported accuracy finding, criterion 4 by full medRxiv preprint (not an abstract/poster). Named exclusions do not apply: it builds its own RAG coder rather than merely benchmarking, and the text coded is patient clinical documentation.
screened.evidence_quote: This study examines whether LLMs can understand and accurately predict mental health-related medical codes from clinical notes.
screened.coder_mechanism: LLM + RAG. Proprietary and open LLMs (GPT, LLaMA, Gemini-Pro) in zero-shot and retrieval-augmented configurations, with ICD-10-CM guidelines and psychiatric diagnostic manuals as the retrieval corpus: "To address the limitations of LLMs, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was leveraged to enhance their performance. By integrating external knowledge sources such as ICD-10-CM guidelines and psychiatric diagnostic manuals, RAG enables LLMs to retrieve relevant information in real time to support their predictions." No supervised encoder/classifier is the coder.
screened.text_type: Psychiatric clinical notes (real-world clinical narratives about patients) — "their ability to identify and understand mental health terms and ICD-10-CM codes in psychiatric clinical notes." Target terminology is ICD-10-CM.
screened.note: DOI landing page (medrxiv.org) returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch; abstract obtained verbatim and cross-checked from two independent sources — the medRxiv/bioRxiv details API (https://api.biorxiv.org/details/medrxiv/10.1101/2024.12.16.24317648) and Europe PMC REST (abstractText). Both returned identical text, so the abstract is confirmed, not reconstructed. One partial caveat worth flagging for the audit log: part of the evaluation probes whether LLMs "understand" the codes themselves (code semantics), which in isolation would fall under the excluded "LLM interprets or queries existing codes" category. However, this is not the whole study — the stated primary task is predicting ICD-10-CM codes from clinical notes, i.e. assignment to a note, so the record clears criterion 1. The accuracy claim about its own system is negative ("Our findings reveal that current models lack a robust understanding of the meaning and nuances of these codes, limiting their reliability for mental health applications"), but the pre-registered rule requires an accuracy claim, not a favourable one, so criterion 3 is met. Preprint status: medRxiv preprints are full papers and are not among the named format exclusions (conference abstract, poster, editorial, protocol, software deposit, book chapter, front-matter); if the audit protocol separately restricts to peer-reviewed venues, this record would need re-adjudication under that rule. No published journal version was surfaced in the search, so no duplicate-report conflict was identified.
screened.adjudicator_reason: Refutation attempt failed on every axis. (1) Real de-identified psychiatric clinical notes (n=50) from the University of Illinois health system, gold codes from psychiatrists' clinical diagnoses — clinical free text about patients, not synthetic text and not code descriptions. (2) Coder is purely LLM/RAG: GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Flash and LLaMA 3.2 in zero-shot and retrieval-augmented configurations over ICD-10-CM guidelines and psychiatric manuals; no BERT/BioClinicalBERT or any supervised classifier appears in the pipeline, so the commonest error does not apply. (3) I specifically checked the second warned-about error: the evaluation is note-to-code assignment, not code interpretation — two experiments, full ICD-10-CM codes per note and three-digit category codes per note, scored with multi-label metrics (Jaccard, Hamming loss, precision/recall/F1) against EHR gold codes. The "lack a robust understanding of these codes" framing is the paper's interpretation of its own low scores, not a code-description benchmark. (4) Own-system accuracy claims reported (F1 0.730 full codes, 0.83 at three-digit level). (5) Full medRxiv preprint with Abstract, Introduction, Methodology, Results, Discussion, Limitations, Ethical Considerations, References — not an abstract, poster, or protocol. Caveat for the parent: two versions exist under this DOI (v1 2024-12-17, v2 2025-03-12); keep v2 as the fullest version if both surface. Small sample (50 notes) is a quality issue, not an eligibility one.
